analysis.one_liner: Requires drug makers to honor safety-net 340B discounts no matter which pharmacy fills the prescription.
analysis.headline: The Senate bill, with 2 cosponsors, was referred to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee on July 22, 2025 and has seen no hearing, markup, or vote since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill writes into law that drug manufacturers must sell medicines at the discounted 340B price to safety-net hospitals and clinics no matter where the drug is dispensed, including through outside "contract pharmacies," and bars manufacturers from putting conditions on those sales, such as refusing to ship to a contract pharmacy or demanding claims data. It also creates fines of up to $2 million per day for manufacturers that intentionally break the rules. The aim is to stop drugmakers from cutting off the dispensing channels safety-net providers use to reach patients.
analysis.who_benefits: Safety-net hospitals, community health centers, HIV and cancer clinics, and their patients — many of them low-income, uninsured, or rural — keep their access to discounted drugs, including specialty drugs for cancer and multiple sclerosis that often only arrive via mail-order or contract pharmacies. Contract pharmacies, which dispense 340B drugs for a fee, keep their lucrative role. Large hospital systems that are the biggest 340B buyers protect a major revenue stream.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Safety-net providers, their patients, contract pharmacies

how_it_helps.text: Codifies that manufacturers must offer the 340B discount price on drugs bought by covered entities 'regardless of the manner or location in which the drug is dispensed,' covering contract pharmacies explicitly.

Bars manufacturers from placing conditions on 340B purchases — including limiting delivery or dispensing locations, refusing to ship to a pharmacy the covered entity names, requiring compliance assurances, or demanding claims data — unless the Health Secretary approves the condition in advance.

Creates a new enforcement tool: civil monetary penalties of up to $2,000,000 per day for intentional violations of the anti-conditions rule or the contract-pharmacy requirement, and directs the Secretary to write rules within 180 days letting covered entities file formal claims of manufacturer violations.

Protects access to specialty drugs — the bill's findings note these drugs for cancer, rheumatoid arthritis, growth hormone deficiency, and multiple sclerosis usually reach covered entities only through specialty or mail-order pharmacies that can be hundreds of miles away, so contract pharmacy arrangements are often the only means of getting them to patients.

analysis.who_pays: Drug manufacturers, who lose their ability to restrict where 340B-discounted drugs are dispensed and face fines up to $2 million a day for violations. Manufacturers argue they recoup 340B discounts by charging higher prices to other payers, meaning employers and commercially insured patients could absorb some of the cost; the bill includes no requirement that the discounts be passed on to patients directly.
analysis.who_pays_short: Drug manufacturers, and possibly other insured payers

drawbacks.text: The bill forbids manufacturers from requiring claims data or other information as a condition of 340B pricing, which makes it harder to detect 'duplicate discounts' — the same prescription being discounted once through 340B and again through Medicaid or Medicare rebates. This dispute over who bears double-discount losses is the core of the ongoing court fights between manufacturers and the government.

Nothing in the bill requires the savings to reach patients: the 340B program's largest participants are hospital systems, and contract pharmacies take a fee on each 340B prescription, so a large share of the discount money can stay with providers and middlemen. The bill's own findings argue covered entities are 'in the best position to assess' how to use savings, rather than directing savings to patient costs.

The penalty provision is unusually steep — up to $2 million per day per violation, assessed each day until the violation ends — which gives the executive branch wide discretion over a major industry and could invite litigation over whether the sanctions are proportionate.

To the extent manufacturers cannot limit 340B dispensing, their stated response has been to raise prices elsewhere in the system, so some of the cost could shift onto commercially insured patients and employers rather than stay with the manufacturers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem: manufacturers have been cutting off contract pharmacies, which for many safety-net clinics and rural patients are the only practical way to get discounted drugs, especially specialty drugs. Patients at community health centers genuinely benefit. But the bill also locks in the 340B system as it actually works today — with large hospital systems capturing much of the discount revenue and contract pharmacy intermediaries taking a fee on every script — while providing no mechanism to verify that savings reach patients and no way for manufacturers to police duplicate discounts. A more balanced version would pair the anti-restriction mandate with transparency or pass-through requirements; this bill resolves the dispute entirely in favor of the covered entities and their pharmacy partners.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee in July 2025, and the committee has taken no action on it since.

narrative.text: Sen. Peter Welch introduced the bill on July 22, 2025, for himself and Sen. Jeff Merkley as original cosponsor.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions.
As of the latest recorded action, the committee has held no hearing or markup and the Senate has held no vote; the bill sits with two cosponsors, both Democrats.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Drug manufacturers, so far: because the bill has not moved, the restrictions they have imposed on shipping 340B-discounted drugs to contract pharmacies remain in force under current policy and court rulings.

for.name: Sen. Peter Welch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sponsored it in the Senate.

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Original cosponsor; the bill was introduced 'for himself and Mr. Merkley.'

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction, chaired by Sen. Bill Cassidy (R-LA)
against.what_they_did: Has taken no action since the bill was referred on July 22, 2025 — no hearing, markup, or vote is recorded.

against.name: Pharmaceutical manufacturers (including Eli Lilly, Bristol Myers Squibb, Sanofi, Johnson & Johnson, Novo Nordisk)
against.what_they_did: Have restricted or refused to ship 340B-discounted drugs to contract pharmacies and oppose codifying a mandate to dispense through them, arguing the arrangements invite duplicate discounts and channel savings to hospitals rather than patients. Their position drives the dispute this bill would settle, though no senator has acted against the bill in the record.

sides.party_line_note: Only Democrats (2) have cosponsored and there have been no votes, but 340B contract-pharmacy legislation has historically attracted Republican support in the House, so the eventual split is unknown.

industries.note: Manufacturers would have to honor the 340B discount in every dispensing channel, could not attach conditions such as refusing to ship to contract pharmacies or demanding claims data, and would face fines up to $2 million a day. Their gain from restricting discounts comes at the direct expense of safety-net providers' and patients' access to discounted drugs.

industries.industry: Contract pharmacies (chains and PBM-affiliated pharmacy networks)
industries.note: The bill writes contract pharmacy arrangements into the 340B statute itself, permanently locking in their role as the dispensing channel for safety-net drugs and the fee stream that comes with it. They expand access points for patients in pharmacy deserts, but they also capture a share of every discounted prescription.

Hospitals are the largest 340B purchasers, and guaranteeing that discounts flow through contract pharmacies protects a major revenue stream they use to fund services — and, critics note, margins. Patients at those hospitals benefit from the access the bill preserves.

industries.industry: Community health centers and safety-net clinics
industries.note: These entities serve low-income, uninsured, and rural patients, and the bill's findings describe 340B savings as letting them 'stretch scarce resources' to reach more patients; the bill preserves the discount channel they depend on.

analysis.trajectory: Most Senate bills referred to committee never reach a vote, and this one has two cosponsors and no committee action five months in. It would need the HELP Committee to hold a markup and party leaders to schedule floor time. The 340B dispute has drawn attention from both parties, so a version of this idea could get attached to a broader drug-pricing or pharmacy-benefits package, but as a standalone bill its odds of a floor vote in this Congress look low.
